scenes.caption: Without an eval you only remember the impressive examples. With one, you can say whether a change helped or hurt.
Illustrative: ten friendly tickets look great. A 50-case eval from past tickets shows invented warranty terms in 8.
Use real past cases, include hard and sensitive ones, define a good answer in writing, and keep a held-back set.
Re-run it every time you change the prompt, the model or the documents.
Have a person score a sample, not only another AI.
Vague prompts get plausible, generic results. Clear ones make the result checkable.
Write it like a brief for a capable new colleague: goal, inputs, rules, what to do when unsure, output format.
Add one or two examples of good output.
Illustrative: 'If a field is not in the thread, write NOT STATED.' Without it, the model fills gaps with plausible guesses.
Automation bias: over-relying on automated suggestions, even when other evidence points the other way.
It shows up two ways: acting on a wrong recommendation, and missing a problem the system didn't flag.
A reviewer who sees only the AI's answer, under time pressure, mostly confirms it.
Have reviewers form their own answer before seeing the AI's, and track how often they disagree.
Myth: a quick paste into a popular AI tool is harmless. Reality: where the text goes depends on product, settings and contract.
Pasted text may be stored, logged, reviewed or, on some plans, used for training.
Illustrative: a full ticket with name, phone and vehicle registration is pasted for a summary that needed none of them.
The safe habit: remove names, phone numbers, addresses and IDs first, and use only approved tools.
Responsible AI is mostly trade-offs, not slogans.
Tuned to never say anything wrong, it refuses or hedges more. Tuned to always help, it sometimes answers when it shouldn't.
The same goes for speed versus review, privacy versus personalisation, and transparency versus simplicity.
Decide which error is costlier in this use, set the threshold on purpose, write the choice down, and revisit it.
A model sounds fluent whether or not it has solid grounds. People do something similar; we call it confidence.
Nothing in the tone reveals which is which. Confidence is a poor guide to accuracy.
Illustrative: an engineer states a root cause with total certainty, the team moves on, and later logs show a different cause.
One rule for both: ask 'what is that based on?' and judge by evidence and track record, not delivery.
In a workflow, code decides the steps in advance. Illustrative: classify the ticket, fetch the device record, draft a reply.
In an agent, the model decides its own steps and which tools to use, looping until it finishes.
Workflows are more predictable, cheaper and easier to test. Agents suit open-ended problems, at the cost of control.
Start with the simplest design, and add autonomy only when it measurably improves results.
Most AI services charge by tokens and take longer the more there are.
An agent re-sends its growing history at each step, so wasteful context multiplies. The shape is schematic.
Illustrative: pass the last three related cases and a short summary, not two years of tickets. Sizes are schematic.
Trim to what is relevant, summarise old steps, ask for concise output, then check answers against your eval set.
Ward Cunningham's 1992 metaphor: shipping code that reflects incomplete understanding is like borrowing. You get speed now.
The interest is the extra effort every later change costs while the gap remains. The curve is schematic.
Paying it down means refactoring once you learn more.
It was never an excuse for knowingly poor work. It was about being honest that understanding grows.
Build: control and fit, but you carry maintenance for good. Buy: working features sooner, on the vendor's design and terms.
No study settles this. The honest answer is that it depends on what is distinctive about you.
Many teams buy the commodity parts and build the thin layer that encodes how their business actually works.
A dashboard that stays green while customers suffer is worse than none.
Google's SRE book suggests four golden signals. Good signals describe what the user experiences, not only server health.
Illustrative: every server shows healthy, yet activations hang. Only request-to-active time reveals a step queueing.
Observability lets you ask new questions about failures you did not predict, not just alert on known ones.
Illustrative: three squads each build a device-health script, with different formats and bugs. One shared service serves all.
A good platform has clear interfaces, documentation and an owner, and treats other teams as its customers.
The risks: building too early for imagined needs, or too rigidly so teams work around it. Start from repeated real demand.
Conway (1968): organisations that design systems tend to produce designs that copy their communication structure.
Illustrative: separate hardware, firmware and app teams talk mainly through tickets.
Customers get three different 'device offline' messages from three systems, none aware of the others.
Use it as a diagnostic, or deliberately: shape teams around the outcome you want, and the architecture tends to follow.
Edmondson was surprised that some better-led hospital teams appeared to record more medication errors.
Her interpretation: they weren't making more mistakes. They were more willing to report them.
A shared belief the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, without fear of embarrassment or punishment.
Illustrative: Pod A logs eight process slips a month, Pod B logs zero. Rewarding Pod B may be rewarding concealment.
A language model generates text by predicting likely next pieces, based on patterns learned in training.
It has no built-in signal that separates 'I know this' from 'this sounds right'.
Illustrative: asked for a refund policy, it gives a plausible clause number. The clause doesn't exist; the tone gave no hint.
For one AI task, require the answer to quote the exact source passage it relied on, then check that passage.
Two ways to make an AI know your business: train it further, or hand it the documents when the question arrives.
Fine-tuning trains the model further on your examples, changing its weights. Good for a style, format or narrow skill.
RAG leaves the model unchanged. At question time it fetches relevant documents and puts them in the prompt.
For facts that change, RAG is usually better: update the documents instead of retraining, and show which source was used.
Imagine the plan has already failed badly. Each person writes down the most likely reasons why.
You are no longer the person doubting the plan. You are answering a question everyone was asked.
Collect reasons silently first, then discuss, so nobody anchors on the most senior person's view.
Illustrative: two leads independently write 'night shift was never trained', a gap no one had mentioned.
"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Strathern's phrasing of Goodhart's idea.
Judge agents on time-to-first-reply, and the fastest path is a quick acknowledgement that says nothing.
The metric turns green while the customer waits exactly as long for an actual answer.
Pair each SLA with a quality check: sample five compliant cases a week. Did the first reply move the case forward?
Index funds try to match a market at low cost. Active funds try to beat it through selection and timing, usually at higher cost.
Before costs, active investors as a group earn roughly the market return. After costs, the average must trail. Schematic.
The open question: can you identify, in advance, the minority who will outperform?
Education, not advice: look up each fund's expense ratio and write its annual cost in rupees next to it.
Investors diversify so one holding failing doesn't sink the portfolio. Teams have the same exposure in people.
When one engineer is the only person who understands the billing integration, the team is 'concentrated'.
Spreading knowledge costs a little efficiency now to reduce a large, sudden loss later — the same trade an investor makes.
List your top five critical skills and how many people can do each without help. Anything with '1' gets a pairing plan.
Myth: waiting for a second marshmallow strongly predicts later success. Reality: the link looks much weaker.
A larger 2018 replication found a much weaker link, which shrank further once background was accounted for. Sizes schematic.
Kidd, Palmeri and Aslin (2013): children waited less after an experimenter had been unreliable.
Still debated, so read famous findings carefully: who was sampled, has it replicated, and what happens when background is controlled?
Approving every step slows an agent and trains people to click 'approve' without reading. That is as useless as reviewing nothing.
Put checkpoints where mistakes are costly or hard to undo. Any 'yes' earns a human review.
Illustrative: the agent drafts replies and tags cases freely, but a human approves refunds, deletions and promised dates.
A checkpoint approved 100% of the time for months is either unnecessary or not being read.
